Handout: Retrieval practice study (sample) 
This is a sample handout used to demonstrate that text inside attached PDFs is
searchable. 
Conditions 
1. Study, study, study, study (rereading only)
2. Study, test, test, test (retrieval practice)
After one week, the retrieval group recalled substantially more. One proposed
mechanism is that effortful recall strengthens consolidation in the hippocampus

notes/20260903-1015-ahrens-three-kinds-o.text:
---
id: "202609031015"
title: "Ahrens: three kinds of notes"
type: literature
tags: [zettelkasten]
source: "202609010900"
created: 2026-09-03T10:15:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-03T10:15:00-04:00
status: active
---

Ahrens separates notes by what they are for:

- **Fleeting notes** are quick reminders of a thought. They are thrown away once processed.
- **Literature notes** are short, selective summaries of a text, in your own words, with the reference.
- **Permanent notes** are written for your future self: one idea, fully formulated, linked into the slip-box.

My take: the point is not the categories but the *processing step* that turns the first two into the third. See [[202609061110|Fleeting notes are reminders, not knowledge]].

notes/20260903-1040-ahrens-from-notes-to.text:
---
id: "202609031040"
title: "Ahrens: from notes to a paper"
type: literature
tags: [writing, zettelkasten]
source: "202609010900"
created: 2026-09-03T10:40:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-03T10:40:00-04:00
status: active
attachments:
  - hash: sha256-6ccc13b452df8f33fc6a17f64ab342719b2d546aa8db5f9ebd810fb22837eb82
    name: workflow.png
    kind: image
    size: 15011
---

The workflow, as I understand it:

1. Capture fleeting notes.
2. Make literature notes while reading.
3. Write permanent notes, linking each to related ones.
4. File them in the slip-box; add links from an index note.
5. Let topics develop bottom-up instead of brainstorming one.
6. Pick a topic once enough notes have gathered around it.
7. Turn the notes into a rough draft.
8. Edit and proofread.

![workflow.png](attachment:6ccc13b452df8f33fc6a17f64ab342719b2d546aa8db5f9ebd810fb22837eb82)

Steps 5 and 6 are the surprising part: see [[202609071000|Topics emerge bottom-up from clusters]].

notes/20260904-1930-kadavy-a-digital-sli.text:
---
id: "202609041930"
title: "Kadavy: a digital slip-box should be non-hierarchical"
type: literature
tags: [zettelkasten, tools]
source: "202609010905"
created: 2026-09-04T19:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-04T19:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

Kadavy warns against copying folder habits into a Zettelkasten. Notes should be reachable through many routes (links, tags, search) rather than living in one place.

He also stresses doing small things on a phone: reviewing, tagging and linking a single note in a spare few minutes.

Related: [[202609101000|Index notes are entry points, not folders]].

notes/20260905-2100-make-it-stick-testin.text:
---
id: "202609052100"
title: "Make It Stick: testing beats rereading"
type: literature
tags: [learning, memory]
source: "202609010910"
created: 2026-09-05T21:00:00-04:00

The authors summarise many experiments where students who quizzed themselves remembered far more a week later than students who reread the same material, even though rereaders *felt* more confident.

The attached handout lists the study conditions.

notes/20260905-2130-make-it-stick-mixing.text:
---
id: "202609052130"
title: "Make It Stick: mixing problem types"
type: literature
tags: [learning]
source: "202609010910"
created: 2026-09-05T21:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-05T21:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

Practising a mix of problem types (interleaving) feels slower and messier than practising one type at a time (blocking), but leads to better results on later tests, because you learn to tell *which* method a problem needs.

notes/20260906-1000-notes-become-valuabl.text:
---
id: "202609061000"
title: Notes become valuable through their connections
type: permanent
tags: [zettelkasten]
created: 2026-09-06T10:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-06T10:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

A single note is just a thought. Its value grows with every link, because each link is a path by which the idea can resurface in a new context.

This is why linking should be effortless and constant, not an afterthought: see [[202609071030|Linking forces you to think about relationships]].

Contrast with folders, where a note can only live in one place: [[202609101000]].

notes/20260906-1020-writing-in-your-own-.text:
---
id: "202609061020"
title: Writing in your own words is a test of understanding
type: permanent
tags: [writing, learning]
created: 2026-09-06T10:20:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-06T10:20:00-04:00
status: active
---

Copying a sentence feels like learning but asks nothing of you. Rephrasing forces you to decide what the text actually means, and reveals immediately when you don't know.

It is a form of [[202609091030|elaboration]], and it guards against [[202609091100|the illusion of fluency]].

notes/20260906-1045-one-idea-per-note.md.text:
---
id: "202609061045"
title: One idea per note
type: permanent
tags: [zettelkasten]
created: 2026-09-06T10:45:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-06T10:45:00-04:00
status: active
---

If a note holds one idea, it can be linked precisely and reused in many arguments. A note with three ideas can only be linked as a bundle.

Rule of thumb: if the title needs "and", split the note.

Links: [[202609061000]] · [[202609101030]]

notes/20260906-1110-fleeting-notes-are-r.text:
---
id: "202609061110"
title: Fleeting notes are reminders, not knowledge
type: permanent
tags: [zettelkasten]
created: 2026-09-06T11:10:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-06T11:10:00-04:00
status: active
---

A fleeting note only has to hold a thought long enough for me to process it, ideally within a day or two. Kept forever, they pile up into an unsearchable mess.

That's what the **Inbox** is for: process each one into a literature or permanent note, or let it go.

Source idea: [[202609031015|Ahrens: three kinds of notes]].

notes/20260907-1000-topics-emerge-bottom.text:
---
id: "202609071000"
title: Topics emerge bottom-up from clusters of notes
type: permanent
tags: [writing, zettelkasten]
created: 2026-09-07T10:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-07T10:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

Instead of choosing a topic and then researching it, keep writing permanent notes about whatever interests you. Over time, some areas become dense with links: those clusters are your topics.

Choosing a topic this way means you start writing with material already in hand: [[202609101030|Drafting from notes avoids the blank page]].

See also [[202609061000]].

notes/20260907-1030-linking-forces-you-t.text:
---
id: "202609071030"
title: Linking forces you to think about relationships
type: permanent
tags: [zettelkasten, learning]
created: 2026-09-07T10:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-07T10:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

When I add a link I have to answer: *how* does this relate? Does it support, contradict, extend, or give an example? That question is where a lot of real thinking happens.

It is also a kind of [[202609091030|elaboration]].

notes/20260908-1000-retrieval-practice-s.text:
---
id: "202609081000"
title: Retrieval practice strengthens memory
type: permanent
tags: [learning, memory]
created: 2026-09-08T10:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-08T10:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

Testing yourself on material works better than rereading it. The effort of recalling strengthens the memory and shows what you don't know yet.

It works best combined with the [[202609081030|spacing effect]], and it is one of the [[202609081130|desirable difficulties]].

From [[202609052100|Make It Stick: testing beats rereading]]. #study

notes/20260908-1030-spacing-effect.md.text:
---
id: "202609081030"
title: Spacing effect
type: permanent
tags: [learning, memory]
created: 2026-09-08T10:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-08T10:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

Spreading practice over time beats cramming it into one session. A bit of forgetting between sessions makes the next recall harder, and that difficulty is what makes it stick.

Pairs with [[202609081000]]. Example of [[202609081130]].

notes/20260908-1100-interleaving-beats-b.text:
---
id: "202609081100"
title: Interleaving beats blocked practice
type: permanent
tags: [learning]
created: 2026-09-08T11:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-08T11:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

Mixing different kinds of problems feels less productive but teaches you to recognise which approach each problem needs.

From [[202609052130]]. Another [[202609081130|desirable difficulty]].

notes/20260908-1130-desirable-difficulti.text:
---
id: "202609081130"
title: Desirable difficulties
type: permanent
tags: [learning, memory]
created: 2026-09-08T11:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-08T11:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

Some kinds of difficulty during learning improve long-term retention, even though they make learning feel slower:

- [[202609081000|Retrieval practice]]
- [[202609081030|Spacing]]
- [[202609081100|Interleaving]]

The trap is that easy methods *feel* better: [[202609091100]].

notes/20260909-1000-writing-is-the-mediu.text:
---
id: "202609091000"
title: Writing is the medium of thinking
type: permanent
tags: [writing]
created: 2026-09-09T10:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-09T10:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

Writing isn't only the output of thinking; it is where much of the thinking happens. Ideas that seem clear in my head often fall apart on the page, which is exactly why it's worth writing them down.

Connects to [[202609061020]] and [[202609101030]].

notes/20260909-1030-elaboration-connects.text:
---
id: "202609091030"
title: Elaboration connects new knowledge to what you know
type: permanent
tags: [learning]
created: 2026-09-09T10:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-09T10:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

Explaining a new idea in terms of things you already know, or finding examples from your own life, gives the memory more hooks.

In a slip-box, every link you add is a small act of elaboration: [[202609071030]].

notes/20260909-1100-rereading-creates-an.text:
---
id: "202609091100"
title: Rereading creates an illusion of fluency
type: permanent
tags: [learning, memory]
created: 2026-09-09T11:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-09T11:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

Familiar text feels easy to read, and we mistake that ease for knowing it. Self-testing breaks the illusion.

See [[202609081000]] and [[202609061020]].

notes/20260910-1000-index-notes-are-entr.text:
---
id: "202609101000"
title: Index notes are entry points, not folders
type: permanent
tags: [zettelkasten, tools]
created: 2026-09-10T10:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-10T10:00:00-04:00
status: active
---

An index note links to a handful of notes in a meaningful order, like a table of contents for one line of thought. Unlike a folder, it doesn't own those notes: each can appear in many indexes.

Examples in this vault: [[202609120930]] and [[202609121000]].

notes/20260910-1030-drafting-from-notes-.text:
---
id: "202609101030"
title: Drafting from notes avoids the blank page
type: permanent
tags: [writing]
created: 2026-09-10T10:30:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-10T10:30:00-04:00
status: active
---

If the permanent notes already exist, a first draft is mostly arranging and connecting them, not producing text from nothing.

The project note [[202609150900]] is an example of an outline built from notes.

notes/20260912-0900-start-here.md.text:
---
id: "202609120900"
title: Start here
type: index
tags: [help]
created: 2026-09-12T09:00:00-04:00
modified: 2026-09-12T09:00:00-04:00
status: active
pinned: true
---

Welcome to the sample slip-box. These notes are about learning and the Zettelkasten method itself.

**Try this:**

1. Tap the **+** button and capture a quick thought. It goes to your **Inbox**.
2. Open **Inbox** and process the notes there: make them permanent, keep, archive or delete.
3. Open a note and scroll down to its **Backlinks**: every note that links to it.
4. Edit a note and type `[[` to link to another note, or `#` to add a tag.
5. Turn your phone sideways in **Review** to see a note and its links side by side, then swipe.
6. Search for the brain region named in the PDF handout attached to a literature note (it starts with h-i-p-p-o). Search reads text inside attachments too.

**Entry points:**

- [[202609121000|The Zettelkasten method]]
- [[202609120930|Learning and memory]]
- [[202609150900|Essay draft: why I keep a slip-box]]
